post.title: Your will doesn't decide who gets your 401(k)
post.ig:
Your will doesn't decide who gets your 401(k).

ERISA plans pay whoever the plan documents and beneficiary form say. If you're married, your spouse generally gets it unless they signed a waiver witnessed by a notary or plan rep.
No form? Many plans default to spouse, then children, then your estate (each plan sets its own order). An estate can mean probate, and if death came before required withdrawals began, generally 5 years to empty the account vs. 10 for most named non-spouse heirs.
The Supreme Court sided with ex-spouses still on the form in Egelhoff v. Egelhoff (2001) and Kennedy v. DuPont (2009, 9-0), where the ex-wife had waived the money in her divorce.

Sources: Egelhoff v. Egelhoff (2001), Kennedy v. Plan Administrator for DuPont (2009), IRS, IRC 417(a)(2).

Your will doesn't decide who gets your 401(k): ERISA plans follow the plan documents and beneficiary form, and a spouse is generally the default unless they signed a notarized or plan-witnessed waiver. With no form, many plans default to spouse, children, then the estate, which can mean probate and, if death came before required withdrawals began, generally a 5-year payout clock vs. 10 years for most named non-spouse heirs (IRS). The Supreme Court sided with ex-spouses still on the form in Egelhoff v. Egelhoff (2001) and Kennedy v. DuPont (2009). News and education, not financial advice.
